sections.title: Components, JSX & Composition
sections.description: Build declarative UI trees with pure components, props, children, and fragments.

lessons.title: JSX Compilation & Pure Rendering
lessons.summary: JSX compiles into lightweight plain JS element objects (`jsx(type, props)`), not live DOM nodes.
explanation: JSX compiles into lightweight plain JS element objects (`jsx(type, props)`), not live DOM nodes.
Components must stay pure during render so identical props and state always produce identical UI, even under StrictMode double-invocation.
Never mutate props or trigger network requests directly in the component body.

codeExample.title: Pure Functional Component

keyPoints: JSX produces plain descriptor objects, not DOM mutations.
PascalCase distinguishes custom components from HTML tags.
Use Fragments (`<>...</>`) to avoid unnecessary wrapper divs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating a prop array during render (`props.items.sort()`)
commonMistakes.fix: Clone before sorting (`[...props.items].sort()`) to keep renders pure.

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming a component in lowercase (`function card()`)
commonMistakes.fix: JSX treats lowercase names as native HTML tags; always PascalCase components.

interviewQA.question: Why does React StrictMode double-invoke components in dev?
interviewQA.answer: To expose impure render logic and side effects early before concurrent features cause bugs.

interviewQA.question: Difference between a React Component and a React Element?
interviewQA.answer: A Component is a function/class; an Element is the immutable plain object returned by JSX.

lessons.title: Props, Children & Composition
lessons.summary: Data flows strictly top-down via read-only props; compose flexible shells using `children` and named slot props.
explanation: Data flows strictly top-down via read-only props; compose flexible shells using `children` and named slot props.
Composition also prevents unnecessary re-renders because `children` JSX created by a parent keeps the same element reference when wrapper state updates.
Prefer composable primitives accepting `children` over bloated 20-prop monolith components.

codeExample.title: Slot-Based Card Composition

keyPoints: Props are read-only inputs owned by the parent.
Children composition avoids deep prop drilling.
Request parent changes via callback props (`onSelect`, `onSave`).

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating `props.title = "X"` directly
commonMistakes.fix: Treat props as immutable and notify the parent via callback props.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding 15 boolean flags to customize one card
commonMistakes.fix: Compose sub-elements via `children` and slot props cleanly.

interviewQA.question: Why does React favor Composition over Inheritance?
interviewQA.answer: Component composition via `children` and props handles layout and behavior variations without fragile class hierarchies.

interviewQA.question: How does passing `children` help performance?
interviewQA.answer: The parent creates the `children` element, so wrapper-local state changes reuse the identical `children` reference.

lessons.title: Conditional Rendering & The Zero-Leak Pitfall
lessons.summary: Use ternaries, early returns, and boolean `&&` expressions for conditional UI.
explanation: Use ternaries, early returns, and boolean `&&` expressions for conditional UI.
In JSX, `false`, `null`, and `undefined` render nothing—but numeric `0` renders a visible `"0"` character!
Always write `items.length > 0 && <List />` instead of `items.length && <List />`.

codeExample.title: Safe Numeric Guard in JSX

keyPoints: null, undefined, true, and false render nothing.
0 and NaN render as literal text nodes.
Early returns flatten loading, error, and empty states cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `{items.length && <List />}`
commonMistakes.fix: When empty, `0 && ...` renders `"0"` on screen; compare `items.length > 0`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stacking 4 nested ternaries in JSX
commonMistakes.fix: Extract a helper component or early-return branches.

interviewQA.question: Why does `{0 && <Badge />}` print `"0"` in React?
interviewQA.answer: JS short-circuits `&&` to return `0`, and React renders numbers as text nodes.

interviewQA.question: When is an early return cleaner than inline ternaries?
interviewQA.answer: For top-level loading, error, and empty page states.

lessons.title: Lists & Stable Key Reconciliation
lessons.summary: Keys let React match list items across inserts, deletions, and reorders to preserve state and minimize DOM edits.
explanation: Keys let React match list items across inserts, deletions, and reorders to preserve state and minimize DOM edits.
Using array index as a `key` on mutable lists corrupts input focus and checkbox states when items shift indices.
Always key items by a stable unique entity ID (`course.slug`, `lesson.id`), never `Math.random()`.

codeExample.title: Stable Entity Keys in Lists

keyPoints: Keys must be unique among siblings, not globally.
Never use `Math.random()` as a key—it remounts on every render.
Intentionally changing a component’s `key` cleanly resets all its local state.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `key={index}` on a list with delete/sort/inputs
commonMistakes.fix: Use stable record IDs so state stays bound to the right item.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `key={Math.random()}`
commonMistakes.fix: Destroys DOM nodes and input focus on every single render.

interviewQA.question: Why is `key={index}` harmful on reorderable lists with inputs?
interviewQA.answer: Deleting item 0 shifts old item 1 into key 0, reusing the wrong DOM input state.

interviewQA.question: When is changing a `key` prop intentionally useful?
interviewQA.answer: Resetting a form or quiz (`<Quiz key={sectionId} />`) cleanly when switching records.

sections.title: State, Events & Immutable Updates
sections.description: Master useState snapshots, functional updaters, immutable updates, and derived state.

lessons.title: useState Snapshots & Functional Updaters
lessons.summary: State acts as a frozen snapshot per render; `setState` schedules the next render rather than mutating the current variable.
explanation: State acts as a frozen snapshot per render; `setState` schedules the next render rather than mutating the current variable.
React 18+ batches state updates automatically even inside `setTimeout` and Promises; pass `(prev) => prev + 1` whenever updates depend on prior state.
Pass a lazy initializer `useState(() => readStorage())` so expensive reads run once on mount.

codeExample.title: Batched Functional Updaters

keyPoints: State variables stay constant within a render’s closure.
Functional updaters `(prev) => next` chain cleanly inside batched updates.
Lazy initializers skip expensive computation on re-renders.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `setN(n + 1); setN(n + 1);` expecting +2
commonMistakes.fix: Both read the same snapshot `n`; use functional updaters `setN((x) => x + 1)`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `useState(parseHugeJson())` directly
commonMistakes.fix: Wrap in an arrow `useState(() => parseHugeJson())` so it runs only once.

interviewQA.question: Why does `console.log(n)` right after `setN(n + 1)` log the old value?
interviewQA.answer: `n` is a const snapshot for the active render; the new value arrives on the next render.

interviewQA.question: What does React 18 Automatic Batching do?
interviewQA.answer: Groups multiple `setState` calls—even inside async callbacks and timers—into a single re-render.

lessons.title: Immutable Object & Array Updates
lessons.summary: React checks state equality via `Object.is`; mutating objects or arrays in place preserves the reference and skips re-rendering.
explanation: React checks state equality via `Object.is`; mutating objects or arrays in place preserves the reference and skips re-rendering.
Use object spread (`{ ...prev, done: true }`) and non-mutating array operations (`map`, `filter`, `[...arr, item]`, `toSorted`).
Keep normalized flat maps (`Record<string, Progress>`) so immutable updates stay shallow and readable.

codeExample.title: Immutable Record Update

keyPoints: Never call `.push()`, `.splice()`, or `.sort()` directly on React state.
`Object.is(prev, next)` must be false for React to commit updates.
Shallow-copy every object along the modified nested path.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating `items.push(x); setItems(items);`
commonMistakes.fix: Reference didn’t change so React bails out; write `setItems((prev) => [...prev, x])`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Copying only the top object while mutating a nested array
commonMistakes.fix: Copy both the outer object and the modified inner array cleanly.

interviewQA.question: Why does mutating state in place fail to trigger a re-render?
interviewQA.answer: React compares previous and next references using `Object.is`, which returns `true` for the mutated same reference.

interviewQA.question: Which array methods are safe for React state updates?
interviewQA.answer: `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`, spread, and ES2023 `toSorted`/`toReversed`/`with`.

lessons.title: Derived State & Lifting State Up
lessons.summary: Never store values in `useState` that can be computed directly from existing props or state during render.
explanation: Never store values in `useState` that can be computed directly from existing props or state during render.
When sibling components need shared state, lift it to their closest common ancestor and pass state + update callbacks down.
Store minimal canonical IDs (`selectedSlug`) instead of duplicating whole objects in state.

codeExample.title: Derived Filter During Render

keyPoints: Derived values stay 100% in sync with zero extra render passes.
Lifting state up establishes a single source of truth.
Avoid copying props into state via `useEffect`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Syncing `filteredItems` in `useState` via `useEffect`
commonMistakes.fix: Triggers a redundant stale render; derive directly during render.

commonMistakes.mistake: Duplicating an entire `activeCourse` object in state
commonMistakes.fix: Store `activeSlug` and derive the course from your catalog list.

interviewQA.question: Why is mirroring derived state via `useEffect` an anti-pattern?
interviewQA.answer: It renders stale UI first, then runs an extra effect and second render, while risking synchronization bugs.

interviewQA.question: What is Lifting State Up?
interviewQA.answer: Moving shared state to the lowest common parent of sibling components that need synchronized data.

lessons.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Forms
lessons.summary: Controlled inputs bind `value` + `onChange` to state for live feedback; uncontrolled inputs read values on submit via `new FormData(e.currentTarget)`.
explanation: Controlled inputs bind `value` + `onChange` to state for live feedback; uncontrolled inputs read values on submit via `new FormData(e.currentTarget)`.
Always initialize controlled text state to `""` (never `undefined`) and handle submission on `<form onSubmit>` with `e.preventDefault()`.
Pair every input with `<label htmlFor="...">` for accessible click targets and screen readers.

codeExample.title: Accessible Controlled Form

keyPoints: Initialize controlled inputs to `""`, never `undefined`.
Use `<form onSubmit>` so Enter key submission works natively.
Use `FormData` for zero-rerender submit-only forms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing `value={user.bio}` when `bio` starts `undefined`
commonMistakes.fix: Triggers the uncontrolled-to-controlled warning; write `value={user.bio ?? ""}`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `onClick` on `<button>` instead of `<form onSubmit>`
commonMistakes.fix: Breaks native Enter-key form submission and HTML5 constraint validation.

interviewQA.question: What triggers React’s uncontrolled-to-controlled input warning?
interviewQA.answer: Rendering an input with `value={undefined}` initially and later changing `value` to a string.

interviewQA.question: When is `FormData` better than controlled `useState` inputs?
interviewQA.answer: On large forms where you only validate/read fields upon submission, avoiding re-renders per keystroke.

sections.title: Effects, Refs & Rules of Hooks
sections.description: Synchronize with external systems safely via useEffect, use refs cleanly, and avoid hook-order bugs.

lessons.title: useEffect Synchronization & Cleanup
lessons.summary: `useEffect` synchronizes React with external systems (DOM listeners, timers, CodeMirror, `document.title`)—not data transformations or click responses.
explanation: `useEffect` synchronizes React with external systems (DOM listeners, timers, CodeMirror, `document.title`)—not data transformations or click responses.
Effects run after paint; return a cleanup function to detach listeners and clear timers before the next run or unmount.
Always keep dependency arrays honest instead of silencing `exhaustive-deps`.

codeExample.title: Window Listener with Cleanup

keyPoints: Effects run after DOM commit and browser paint.
Cleanup runs both before dependency re-runs and on unmount.
Handle user actions in event handlers, not effects.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting changing variables from the dependency array
commonMistakes.fix: Creates stale closures reading outdated props/state.

commonMistakes.mistake: Triggering POST mutations in `useEffect` when a flag changes
commonMistakes.fix: Run mutations directly in `onSubmit` / `onClick` handlers.

interviewQA.question: When does a `useEffect` cleanup function run?
interviewQA.answer: Right before the effect re-runs after a dependency change AND when the component unmounts.

interviewQA.question: Why does StrictMode run mount -> cleanup -> remount in dev?
interviewQA.answer: To catch missing teardown logic and leaked subscriptions early.

lessons.title: Race-Free Async Fetching in Effects
lessons.summary: Rapidly switching `courseSlug` can resolve earlier slow requests AFTER newer fast ones—overwriting fresh data with stale results!
explanation: Rapidly switching `courseSlug` can resolve earlier slow requests AFTER newer fast ones—overwriting fresh data with stale results!
Guard every async effect with `let cancelled = false` or an `AbortController` aborted inside the cleanup callback.
Never write `useEffect(async () => ...)` directly because async functions return a Promise instead of a cleanup function.

codeExample.title: Cancellation-Safe Course Loader

keyPoints: Never pass an `async` function directly to `useEffect`.
Use `AbortController` or a `cancelled` flag to discard stale responses.
Always handle loading, error, and empty states cleanly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `useEffect(async () => { ... }, [id])`
commonMistakes.fix: Define an inner async helper or `.then()` chain so the effect returns a synchronous cleanup function.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring out-of-order fetch completions when params change quickly
commonMistakes.fix: Abort or ignore stale responses in cleanup.

interviewQA.question: Why is `useEffect(async () => ...)` invalid?
interviewQA.answer: Async functions return a Promise, whereas `useEffect` only accepts `void` or a synchronous cleanup callback.

interviewQA.question: How do you prevent race conditions when fetching on `slug` changes?
interviewQA.answer: Create an `AbortController` (or boolean `cancelled` flag) inside the effect and abort/set it inside cleanup.

lessons.title: useRef for DOM Nodes & Mutable Handles
lessons.summary: `useRef(init)` creates a persistent `{ current }` container across renders whose mutation NEVER triggers a re-render.
explanation: `useRef(init)` creates a persistent `{ current }` container across renders whose mutation NEVER triggers a re-render.
Use refs for imperative DOM calls (`.focus()`, `.scrollIntoView()`) and non-visual mutable handles (interval IDs, editor instances).
Never read or write `ref.current` during render; touch refs in effects and event handlers.

codeExample.title: Focusing an Input with useRef
codeExample.code:
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);
<button onClick={() => inputRef.current?.focus()}>Search</button>

keyPoints: Mutating `ref.current` never causes a re-render.
Use `useState` for rendered UI data; `useRef` for imperative handles.
DOM refs populate after commit.

commonMistakes.mistake: Storing a displayed score inside `useRef` expecting UI updates
commonMistakes.fix: Use `useState` for anything shown in JSX.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading `ref.current.clientWidth` directly inside render body
commonMistakes.fix: Read DOM measurements in `useLayoutEffect` or event handlers.

interviewQA.question: Difference between `useState` and `useRef`?
interviewQA.answer: Changing `useState` triggers a re-render with immutable snapshots; mutating `useRef.current` is synchronous and never re-renders.

interviewQA.question: How do you type a DOM input ref in TypeScript?
interviewQA.answer: `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)`.

lessons.title: Rules of Hooks & Fiber Hook Lists
lessons.summary: React identifies hooks strictly by call order inside a linked list on the component’s Fiber node.
explanation: React identifies hooks strictly by call order inside a linked list on the component’s Fiber node.
Therefore hooks must ALWAYS run unconditionally at the top level—never inside `if`, `for`, callbacks, or after an early `return`.
Move conditions inside the hook body (`useEffect(() => { if (!active) return; ... })`).

codeExample.title: Unconditional Top-Level Hooks

keyPoints: Hook order must be identical across every render.
Never call hooks after an early `if (!data) return null;`.
Custom hooks must start with `use` for linter verification.

commonMistakes.mistake: Placing `useState` after `if (loading) return <Spinner />;`
commonMistakes.fix: Call all hooks at the top before any conditional `return`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling hooks inside `.map()`
commonMistakes.fix: Extract each item into a child component with its own top-level hooks.

interviewQA.question: Why does React forbid conditional hook calls?
interviewQA.answer: React stores hook states in a positional linked list on the Fiber; skipping a hook shifts every subsequent hook’s state slot.

interviewQA.question: How do you run an effect conditionally?
interviewQA.answer: Call `useEffect` unconditionally and return early inside its callback when inactive.

sections.title: Custom Hooks, Routing, Error Boundaries & Portals
sections.description: Share stateful logic via custom hooks and structure resilient multi-page SPAs.

lessons.title: Authoring Reusable Custom Hooks
lessons.summary: Custom hooks (`use*`) compose built-in hooks to share stateful behavior without wrapper-component nesting.
explanation: Custom hooks (`use*`) compose built-in hooks to share stateful behavior without wrapper-component nesting.
Crucially, custom hooks share LOGIC, NOT state—every caller gets its own completely isolated state slots.
Only prefix a helper with `use` if it actually calls React hooks internally.

codeExample.title: useDebouncedValue Custom Hook

keyPoints: Custom hooks isolate independent state per calling component.
Keep inputs minimal and return tuples (2 items) or objects (3+ items).
Plain utilities without hooks should NOT start with `use`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting two components calling `useTimer()` to share the same seconds value
commonMistakes.fix: Lift state up or use Context to share state; custom hooks share logic only.

commonMistakes.mistake: Naming a pure formatter `useFormatDate`
commonMistakes.fix: Plain helpers have no hook restrictions and work anywhere.

interviewQA.question: Do two components calling the same custom hook share state?
interviewQA.answer: No—each component gets its own independent hook state.

interviewQA.question: Why must custom hooks begin with `use`?
interviewQA.answer: So React’s ESLint plugin enforces Rules of Hooks inside them automatically.

lessons.title: React Router: Nested Layouts, Params & Search Params
lessons.summary: React Router maps URLs to nested `<Route>` trees using `<Outlet />`, `useParams()`, and `useSearchParams()`.
explanation: React Router maps URLs to nested `<Route>` trees using `<Outlet />`, `useParams()`, and `useSearchParams()`.
Use `<Link>` / `<NavLink>` instead of `<a href>` for internal routes so navigation happens instantly without reloading the page.
Store catalog search and filter criteria in `useSearchParams` so URLs are shareable and bookmarkable.

codeExample.title: Nested Layout with Outlet & useParams

keyPoints: `<Outlet />` renders matched child routes inside persistent shells.
`<NavLink>` exposes `isActive` for active navigation styling.
Always define a `<Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />` fallback.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `<a href="/courses">` for internal SPA navigation
commonMistakes.fix: Triggers full browser reloads; use `<Link to="/courses">`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting SPA `index.html` fallback on static hosts
commonMistakes.fix: Direct deep links return 404 on refresh unless routed to `index.html`.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between `<Link>` and `<NavLink>`?
interviewQA.answer: `<NavLink>` knows whether its route is currently active and passes `{ isActive }` to className/style callbacks.

interviewQA.question: What does `<Outlet />` render?
interviewQA.answer: The matched nested child `<Route>` element inside a parent layout route.

lessons.title: Error Boundaries & Graceful Recovery
lessons.summary: An Error Boundary class component (`getDerivedStateFromError` + `componentDidCatch`) prevents a single render crash from blanking the whole application.
explanation: An Error Boundary class component (`getDerivedStateFromError` + `componentDidCatch`) prevents a single render crash from blanking the whole application.
Error Boundaries catch render and lifecycle exceptions in child trees—NOT errors inside event handlers or async callbacks (use `try/catch` there).
Always provide a clear recovery button (Retry / Home) in the fallback UI.

codeExample.title: Minimal Production Error Boundary

keyPoints: Catches render-phase errors in descendant trees cleanly.
Does NOT catch `onClick` or async `setTimeout` throws.
Pair with lazy routes to handle failed chunk downloads gracefully.

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting an Error Boundary to catch an error thrown inside `onClick`
commonMistakes.fix: Catch event handler errors explicitly with `try/catch`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shipping an app with zero Error Boundaries
commonMistakes.fix: Wrap your root router and complex widgets (like code editors) in Error Boundaries.

interviewQA.question: Which errors do React Error Boundaries NOT catch?
interviewQA.answer: Event handler errors, async callbacks/Promises, SSR errors, and errors thrown by the boundary itself.

interviewQA.question: Why is `getDerivedStateFromError` static?
interviewQA.answer: It runs purely during render to transition to fallback state without touching `this` or side effects.

lessons.title: Portals & Accessible Overlay Modals
lessons.summary: `createPortal(node, document.body)` mounts modals/toasts at the top of the DOM—escaping `overflow: hidden` and `z-index` clipping—while preserving React Context and event bubbling!
explanation: `createPortal(node, document.body)` mounts modals/toasts at the top of the DOM—escaping `overflow: hidden` and `z-index` clipping—while preserving React Context and event bubbling!
Accessible overlays support `Escape` dismissal, `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"`, and focus restoration.
Remember that synthetic clicks inside a Portal still bubble up the REACT component hierarchy.

codeExample.title: Portal Modal Escape Hatch

keyPoints: Escapes ancestor `overflow: hidden` and `transform` stacking traps.
Preserves React Context and synthetic event bubbling intact.
Native `<dialog>` with `.showModal()` provides built-in top-layer behavior.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming Portal children lose access to ancestor React Context
commonMistakes.fix: Portals stay connected to the React Fiber tree, so Context works seamlessly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mounting fixed modals inside transformed cards without a Portal
commonMistakes.fix: CSS `transform` traps `position: fixed`; mount via Portal or `<dialog>`.

interviewQA.question: Do React events from a Portal bubble to the React parent component?
interviewQA.answer: Yes—React synthetic events follow the React component tree, not the physical DOM hierarchy.

interviewQA.question: Why do modals clip inside `overflow: hidden` cards without Portals?
interviewQA.answer: DOM descendants inherit ancestor clipping unless mounted at `document.body` via `createPortal` or the browser top layer via `<dialog>.showModal()`.

sections.title: Context API, useReducer & Scalable State
sections.description: Eliminate prop drilling with Context, model state machines with useReducer, and build compound components.

lessons.title: Context API & Memoized Providers
lessons.summary: Context shares cross-cutting state (theme, user, progress) across deep trees without prop drilling.
explanation: Context shares cross-cutting state (theme, user, progress) across deep trees without prop drilling.
Every consumer calling `useContext(Ctx)` re-renders whenever the Provider `value` reference changes—so memoize Provider values with `useMemo`!
Wrap `useContext` in a custom `useApp()` hook that throws clearly outside the Provider.

codeExample.title: Non-Null Memoized Context Provider

keyPoints: Memoize Provider `value` to avoid pointless consumer re-renders.
Every consumer re-renders on any Provider value identity change.
Wrap in a custom hook for clean non-null TypeScript ergonomics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Passing `<Ctx.Provider value={{ a, b }}>` inline without `useMemo`
commonMistakes.fix: Creates a fresh object every parent render, re-rendering every consumer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting high-frequency search input text into RootContext
commonMistakes.fix: Keep ephemeral UI state local or split Contexts cleanly.

interviewQA.question: Why can one giant AppContext cause performance issues?
interviewQA.answer: Changing any single property gives the Provider a new object reference, re-rendering EVERY consumer even if it only reads untouched fields.

interviewQA.question: How do you prevent over-rendering with Context?
interviewQA.answer: Split fast vs slow contexts, separate State from Dispatch, memoize Provider values, or use a selector store.

lessons.title: useReducer for Pure Testable State Machines
lessons.summary: `useReducer` centralizes multi-field transitions (such as a timed exam or multi-step wizard) into one pure function `(state, action) => nextState`.
explanation: `useReducer` centralizes multi-field transitions (such as a timed exam or multi-step wizard) into one pure function `(state, action) => nextState`.
React guarantees `dispatch` keeps a permanently stable function identity across renders—ideal for Context and memoized children.
Extract reducers to standalone `.ts` modules so they can be unit-tested with `node:test` in milliseconds.

codeExample.title: Pure Exam Reducer

keyPoints: Reducers are pure and 100% unit-testable outside React.
`dispatch` never changes reference identity across renders.
Discriminated action unions make invalid transitions impossible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mutating `state.answers[id] = idx` inside a reducer
commonMistakes.fix: Always return new shallow-copied objects immutably.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `fetch()` inside a reducer
commonMistakes.fix: Keep reducers pure; trigger network I/O in event handlers or effects.

interviewQA.question: When is `useReducer` better than several `useState` calls?
interviewQA.answer: When one action updates multiple interdependent fields or when you want pure testable state transitions and stable `dispatch`.

interviewQA.question: Does `dispatch` ever change identity between renders?
interviewQA.answer: No—React guarantees `dispatch` is stable for the component’s entire lifetime.

lessons.title: State Colocation & Splitting State vs Dispatch Contexts
lessons.summary: Colocate state as close to its consumers as possible, store filter/search state in URL searchParams, and separate StateContext from DispatchContext.
explanation: Colocate state as close to its consumers as possible, store filter/search state in URL searchParams, and separate StateContext from DispatchContext.
When action-only buttons consume only `DispatchContext`, state updates never cause those buttons to re-render!
Categorize state intentionally: Local UI, URL state, Server Cache, and Global Client state.

codeExample.title: Split State & Dispatch Contexts

keyPoints: Colocating state minimizes the subtree affected by updates.
URL searchParams make filters bookmarkable and refresh-safe.
Splitting State and Dispatch eliminates re-renders on write-only buttons.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hoisting local dropdown open state into global Context
commonMistakes.fix: Keep ephemeral toggle state inside the dropdown component itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting both changing state and stable actions in one Context when many action-only controls exist
commonMistakes.fix: Split into two Contexts so action-only controls stay static.

interviewQA.question: Why does splitting StateContext and DispatchContext reduce re-renders?
interviewQA.answer: Because `dispatch` never changes reference, consumers of `DispatchContext` never re-render when `StateContext` updates.

interviewQA.question: Why put catalog filters in `useSearchParams` instead of `useState`?
interviewQA.answer: Filters survive page reloads, work with Back/Forward, and can be shared via link.

lessons.title: Compound Components & Headless Patterns
lessons.summary: Compound components (`<Tabs>`, `<Tabs.Trigger>`, `<Tabs.Panel>`) share state implicitly via private Context, allowing clean, flexible JSX layouts at any nesting depth.
explanation: Compound components (`<Tabs>`, `<Tabs.Trigger>`, `<Tabs.Panel>`) share state implicitly via private Context, allowing clean, flexible JSX layouts at any nesting depth.
Headless patterns encapsulate ARIA roles, keyboard navigation, and state while letting callers control visual markup completely.
Prefer private Context over `React.cloneElement` so wrapping triggers in layout divs never breaks coordination.

codeExample.title: Compound Tabs with Private Context

keyPoints: Private Context works through arbitrary intermediate wrapper elements.
Keeps ARIA linkage (`aria-selected`, `role="tabpanel"`) centralized.
Avoids giant configuration-object props.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `React.Children.map` + `cloneElement` for compound APIs
commonMistakes.fix: Breaks the moment a caller adds a wrapper `<div>`; use private Context instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting keyboard arrow navigation in custom tab/menu compounds
commonMistakes.fix: Follow WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices for full keyboard support.

interviewQA.question: Why is private Context superior to `React.cloneElement` for compound components?
interviewQA.answer: Context passes through any depth of layout wrappers without requiring sub-components to be direct children.

interviewQA.question: What is a headless UI component?
interviewQA.answer: A component/hook supplying all state, keyboard logic, and ARIA semantics while leaving styling 100% to the consumer.

lessons.title: Render vs Commit Phases & Reconciliation
lessons.summary: React renders purely in JS (Render phase, interruptible) and applies minimal real DOM diffs synchronously (Commit phase).
explanation: React renders purely in JS (Render phase, interruptible) and applies minimal real DOM diffs synchronously (Commit phase).
Never define a component function inside another component—each render generates a new function identity, forcing React to unmount and remount the child every time!
Remember: a component re-rendering in JS does NOT mean the browser repaints unchanged DOM nodes.

codeExample.title: Stable Module-Level Sub-Component

keyPoints: Different root tag types (`div` -> `section`) unmount and remount the subtree.
Define all components at module scope, never nested inside another component.
Parent re-renders re-render children by default unless memoized or passed as `children`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Declaring `function Row() { ... }` inside `function Table()`
commonMistakes.fix: Causes full unmount/remount on every parent render, wiping input focus and hook state.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming every JS render causes a full DOM rebuild
commonMistakes.fix: Commit phase only touches the specific attributes/text nodes that changed.

interviewQA.question: What happens when you define a component inside another component’s body?
interviewQA.answer: Its function reference changes on every parent render, so React unmounts the old instance and mounts a brand-new one, losing focus and local state.

interviewQA.question: Difference between Render phase and Commit phase?
interviewQA.answer: Render computes the next Fiber tree purely; Commit updates the DOM and runs layout/passive effects.

lessons.title: React.memo, useMemo & useCallback Discipline
lessons.summary: `React.memo` skips child re-renders when props are shallowly equal; `useMemo` caches expensive derived values or object references; `useCallback` stabilizes callback references.
explanation: `React.memo` skips child re-renders when props are shallowly equal; `useMemo` caches expensive derived values or object references; `useCallback` stabilizes callback references.
`React.memo` fails silently if the parent passes un-memoized inline objects (`options={{ a: 1 }}`) or inline callbacks (`onClick={() => ...}`).
Profile with React DevTools before memoizing—pushing state down often solves re-renders more cleanly than memoization.

codeExample.title: Coordinated memo + useMemo + useCallback

keyPoints: `React.memo` compares props via shallow `Object.is`.
`useCallback` only prevents child renders when paired with `React.memo` or effect deps.
Avoid premature memoization on cheap leaf components.

commonMistakes.mistake: Wrapping `Child` in `React.memo` while passing `style={{ padding: 8 }}` inline
commonMistakes.fix: Fresh style object defeats `React.memo` on every render; hoist static objects outside render.

commonMistakes.mistake: Wrapping trivial string math in `useMemo`
commonMistakes.fix: Adds dependency-comparison overhead with zero measurable benefit.

interviewQA.question: Why can a `React.memo` component still re-render on every parent update?
interviewQA.answer: Passing fresh inline objects, arrays, or arrow functions breaks shallow `Object.is` prop equality.

interviewQA.question: What structural refactor often beats `React.memo`?
interviewQA.answer: Moving fast-changing state down into a small leaf component or passing heavy siblings as `children`.

lessons.title: Code Splitting with React.lazy & Suspense
lessons.summary: Route- and feature-level code splitting via `React.lazy(() => import("./Page"))` shrinks initial JS bundles for fast First Contentful Paint.
explanation: Route- and feature-level code splitting via `React.lazy(() => import("./Page"))` shrinks initial JS bundles for fast First Contentful Paint.
Always declare `lazy()` at module top level—never inside render—and wrap `<Suspense fallback={<Skeleton />}>` inside an Error Boundary.
Code-split heavy optional tools (PDF export, CodeMirror editors, charts) cleanly.

codeExample.title: Module-Scope React.lazy & Suspense

keyPoints: `React.lazy` downloads chunks on demand when first rendered.
Declare `lazy()` outside components so identity never resets.
Pair with an Error Boundary to recover from offline chunk failures.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `const P = lazy(() => import(...))` inside a component body
commonMistakes.fix: Recreates the lazy wrapper every render, flashing the fallback endlessly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving `fallback={null}` on slow routes
commonMistakes.fix: Provide a matching skeleton UI to prevent layout shift (CLS).

interviewQA.question: Why must `React.lazy()` be called at module top level?
interviewQA.answer: Calling it inside render generates a fresh lazy wrapper every render, causing repeated remounts and fallback flashes.

interviewQA.question: What export shape does `React.lazy` expect?
interviewQA.answer: A module Promise resolving to `{ default: Component }`.

lessons.title: List Virtualization (Windowing) for Massive Datasets
lessons.summary: Virtualization mounts ONLY the ~15–25 rows currently intersecting the scroll viewport plus overscan, keeping DOM size O(1) even for 100,000 rows.
explanation: Virtualization mounts ONLY the ~15–25 rows currently intersecting the scroll viewport plus overscan, keeping DOM size O(1) even for 100,000 rows.
Position the rendered slice via GPU-composited `transform: translateY(offsetY)` inside a spacer sized to `total * rowHeight`.
Reserve virtualization for genuinely large lists (200+ complex rows) so small lists retain native browser Ctrl+F search.

Provide in-app search when virtualizing because off-screen nodes aren’t in DOM for Ctrl+F.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mounting 10,000 complex table rows directly into the DOM
commonMistakes.fix: Virtualize or paginate so layout/paint stays well under 16ms.

commonMistakes.mistake: Virtualizing a 23-card catalog unnecessarily
commonMistakes.fix: Small grids render natively in <2ms and preserve full native Ctrl+F & accessibility.

interviewQA.question: How does windowing keep 50,000 rows scrolling at 60fps?
interviewQA.answer: It renders an empty spacer for total scroll height while mounting only the ~20 rows visible in the viewport plus overscan.

interviewQA.question: What UX trade-off comes with list virtualization?
interviewQA.answer: Native browser Ctrl+F cannot find unmounted off-screen rows, so pair virtualized views with an in-app search bar.

lessons.title: useTransition & useDeferredValue
lessons.summary: Concurrent React distinguishes urgent updates (typing, clicking) from interruptible transitions (filtering huge lists, switching heavy tabs).
explanation: Concurrent React distinguishes urgent updates (typing, clicking) from interruptible transitions (filtering huge lists, switching heavy tabs).
Keep controlled input state urgent and wrap heavy downstream updates in `startTransition` or derive a deferred value with `useDeferredValue(query)`.
Compare `query !== deferredQuery` to show subtle dimming while background rendering completes.

codeExample.title: Lag-Free Filtering with useDeferredValue

keyPoints: Transitions pause automatically when urgent keystrokes arrive.
Never wrap a controlled input’s own `setText` in `startTransition`.
Pair `useDeferredValue` with `useMemo` or `React.memo` so urgent renders reuse prior results.

commonMistakes.mistake: Wrapping `setInputValue(e.target.value)` inside `startTransition`
commonMistakes.fix: Controlled typing must stay urgent or cursor jumps; defer the filtered view instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `useDeferredValue` without memoizing the heavy computation
commonMistakes.fix: Without `useMemo`/`React.memo`, the heavy work still runs on the urgent keystroke pass.

interviewQA.question: How does `useDeferredValue` differ from debouncing?
interviewQA.answer: Debounce always enforces a fixed wait timer; `useDeferredValue` renders immediately when idle and interrupts mid-render if new input arrives.

interviewQA.question: When choose `useTransition` vs `useDeferredValue`?
interviewQA.answer: Use `useTransition` when you own the `setState` call and want `isPending`; use `useDeferredValue` when deferring a prop or derived value.

lessons.title: React 19 Actions, useActionState & Ref-as-Prop
lessons.summary: React 19 lets async functions run directly via `<form action={fn}>`, tracks pending/error/result automatically with `useActionState`, and accepts `ref` as a regular prop with zero `forwardRef` boilerplate!
explanation: React 19 lets async functions run directly via `<form action={fn}>`, tracks pending/error/result automatically with `useActionState`, and accepts `ref` as a regular prop with zero `forwardRef` boilerplate!
Child submit buttons call `useFormStatus()` to disable automatically while their ancestor `<form>` action is pending.

React 19 functional components accept `ref` directly as a prop.
`useFormStatus()` reads pending status from the nearest parent `<form>`.

commonMistakes.fix: Move `<SubmitButton />` into a child component inside `<form>`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Keeping unnecessary `forwardRef` wrappers in React 19
commonMistakes.fix: Pass `ref` directly via props cleanly.

interviewQA.question: What boilerplate does React 19 remove for refs?
interviewQA.answer: `React.forwardRef` is no longer needed—function components accept `ref` directly in `props`.

interviewQA.question: Why must `useFormStatus()` run in a child component of `<form>`?
interviewQA.answer: It reads status from the nearest ancestor `<form>`, similar to Context.

lessons.title: Optimistic UI with useOptimistic
lessons.summary: `useOptimistic(realState, updateFn)` displays immediate 0ms UI updates while an async action runs, automatically reverting to canonical state if the request fails.
explanation: `useOptimistic(realState, updateFn)` displays immediate 0ms UI updates while an async action runs, automatically reverting to canonical state if the request fails.
Ideal for high-probability toggles (bookmarks, likes, lesson completion checkboxes) paired with an error toast on failure.
Avoid optimistic deletion for irreversible destructive actions—confirm those explicitly.

codeExample.title: Zero-Latency Toggle with useOptimistic

keyPoints: Delivers instant perceived responsiveness for network toggles.
Reverts cleanly to canonical state automatically when the action settles without updating source state.
Always surface a clear error toast if rollback occurs.

commonMistakes.mistake: Silently rolling back a failed optimistic save with zero user feedback
commonMistakes.fix: Display a clear toast explaining that the change failed to save.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `setOptimistic` outside an async transition or action
commonMistakes.fix: Optimistic state overlays belong inside a transition/action lifecycle.

interviewQA.question: How does `useOptimistic` handle failure rollback?
interviewQA.answer: Once the async action finishes without updating canonical props/state, React discards the temporary optimistic overlay automatically.

interviewQA.question: Which interactions fit optimistic UI best?
interviewQA.answer: Frequent reversible toggles like bookmarks, likes, and completion ticks.

lessons.title: Testing Trophy & Clean React Architecture
lessons.summary: Test pure reducers and utilities with fast unit tests (`node:test`), test UI components by accessible roles/labels (`getByRole`, `getByLabelText`), and keep persistence behind a clean adapter layer.
explanation: Test pure reducers and utilities with fast unit tests (`node:test`), test UI components by accessible roles/labels (`getByRole`, `getByLabelText`), and keep persistence behind a clean adapter layer.
Querying by accessible role verifies both user behavior and screen-reader accessibility simultaneously.
Isolate pure business rules (progress math, scoring, unlocking) outside React components so tests run in milliseconds.

keyPoints: Pure domain utils run 100x faster in unit tests than mounted DOM suites.
Query UI by accessible role/label instead of brittle CSS classes.
Abstract storage behind an interface so localStorage -> Supabase swaps in one module.

commonMistakes.mistake: Testing internal hook state or `.btn-indigo` CSS classes
commonMistakes.fix: Assert observable text, states, and ARIA roles so styling refactors never break tests.

commonMistakes.mistake: Scattering raw `localStorage` calls inside 15 components
commonMistakes.fix: Centralize persistence in one storage service module.

interviewQA.question: Why does React Testing Library prefer `getByRole` over `data-testid`?
interviewQA.answer: It verifies that real users and assistive technologies can actually locate and understand the control.

interviewQA.question: Why decouple quiz scoring and certificate eligibility from React components?
interviewQA.answer: Pure functions are deterministic, framework-agnostic, and testable in milliseconds with `node:test`.

lessons.title: useSyncExternalStore for External Subscriptions
lessons.summary: `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` subscribes to browser APIs (`navigator.onLine`, `matchMedia`) or external stores without concurrent UI tearing.
explanation: `useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot)` subscribes to browser APIs (`navigator.onLine`, `matchMedia`) or external stores without concurrent UI tearing.
Remember: `getSnapshot` MUST return a cached/primitive reference when unchanged—returning a fresh `{}` literal every call triggers an infinite render loop!
Provide `getServerSnapshot` whenever supporting SSR to avoid hydration errors.

codeExample.title: Tear-Free Online Status Hook

keyPoints: Prevents concurrent tearing on external mutable stores.
`getSnapshot` must return referentially stable snapshots when unchanged.
Third argument supplies SSR-safe initial snapshot.

commonMistakes.mistake: Returning `() => ({ online: navigator.onLine })` fresh object from `getSnapshot`
commonMistakes.fix: Fails `Object.is` every check and loops infinitely; return primitives or cached objects.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting `getServerSnapshot` in SSR apps
commonMistakes.fix: Causes server render crashes; always provide a deterministic server default.

interviewQA.question: What is UI tearing and how does `useSyncExternalStore` solve it?
interviewQA.answer: Tearing happens when an external store mutates mid-concurrent-render so two components show inconsistent values; `useSyncExternalStore` forces consistent snapshot reads.

interviewQA.question: Why must `getSnapshot` return the same reference when nothing changed?
interviewQA.answer: React compares snapshots with `Object.is` and re-renders infinitely if every call returns a new object literal.

lessons.title: useLayoutEffect vs useEffect
lessons.summary: `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after DOM mutations and BEFORE browser paint—preventing 1-frame visual flicker for tooltip positioning or DOM measurements.
explanation: `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after DOM mutations and BEFORE browser paint—preventing 1-frame visual flicker for tooltip positioning or DOM measurements.
Because it blocks browser painting, keep `useLayoutEffect` tiny and reserve `useEffect` for 99% of side effects (fetching, subscriptions, timers).
Execution order: Render -> DOM commit -> `useLayoutEffect` -> Paint -> `useEffect`.

codeExample.title: Zero-Flicker Tooltip Flip

keyPoints: Runs synchronously before paint to eliminate visual jumps.
Blocks paint—never run slow loops or network calls inside it.
Prefer CSS positioning when possible before reaching for `useLayoutEffect`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Running heavy API calls inside `useLayoutEffect`
commonMistakes.fix: Delays initial paint; move async work to `useEffect`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Measuring & repositioning a tooltip in `useEffect` causing a visible jump
commonMistakes.fix: Move just the geometry measurement to `useLayoutEffect`.

interviewQA.question: Exact execution order of render, `useLayoutEffect`, paint, and `useEffect`?
interviewQA.answer: Render -> DOM commit -> `useLayoutEffect` -> Browser Paint -> `useEffect`.

interviewQA.question: Why does SSR warn about `useLayoutEffect`?
interviewQA.answer: Servers have no DOM layout geometry, so layout effects cannot run until client hydration.

lessons.title: useId for Accessible Collision-Free IDs
lessons.summary: `useId()` produces unique, deterministic, SSR-safe IDs for linking `<label htmlFor={id}>`, `<input id={id}>`, and `aria-describedby={`${id}-hint`}` across multiple component instances.
explanation: `useId()` produces unique, deterministic, SSR-safe IDs for linking `<label htmlFor={id}>`, `<input id={id}>`, and `aria-describedby={`${id}-hint`}` across multiple component instances.
Never use `useId()` for React list `key` props—keys must always derive from stable data identifiers!
Derive multiple related ARIA IDs from one `useId()` base string.

keyPoints: Prevents duplicate HTML `id` collisions when a component renders twice.
Matches identically between SSR HTML and client hydration.
Never use `useId()` as a list `key`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `id={Math.random()}` in form inputs
commonMistakes.fix: Breaks SSR hydration and regenerates on every render; use `useId()`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using `useId()` as a `.map()` `key`
commonMistakes.fix: Keys represent data identity, not tree position.

interviewQA.question: Why shouldn’t `useId()` be used for list `key` props?
interviewQA.answer: Keys must identify data items across moves/deletions; `useId()` tracks render position.

interviewQA.question: How do you derive multiple IDs for one input (hint + error)?
interviewQA.answer: Call `useId()` once and append suffixes like `${id}-hint` and `${id}-error`.

lessons.title: Eliminating Stale Closures in Timers & Listeners
lessons.summary: A stale closure occurs when a callback registered once (`[]` deps) captures outdated state from render 1.
explanation: A stale closure occurs when a callback registered once (`[]` deps) captures outdated state from render 1.
Fix stale closures cleanly with functional updaters (`setSeconds(s => s + 1)`), honest dependency arrays, or a latest-callback ref (`cbRef.current = cb`) for non-restarting intervals.
Always reach for functional updaters first—they solve most timer/counter stale closures in one line.

codeExample.title: Stale-Free Custom useInterval Hook

Latest-ref pattern lets long-lived timers invoke fresh closures without resetting.
Never disable `react-hooks/exhaustive-deps` blindly.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `setInterval(() => setN(n + 1), 1000)` inside `useEffect(..., [])`
commonMistakes.fix: Captures `n = 0` forever so UI freezes at `1`; use `setN((prev) => prev + 1)`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Resetting a 60-second timer every render because an inline callback is in `deps`
commonMistakes.fix: Store the latest callback in a ref or stabilize with `useCallback`.

interviewQA.question: Why does `setN(n + 1)` inside `useEffect(..., [])` get stuck at 1?
interviewQA.answer: The closure captures `n = 0` from initial mount forever, setting `0 + 1` on every tick.

interviewQA.question: How does the latest-ref pattern avoid restarting a WebSocket or timer?
interviewQA.answer: The subscription reads `cbRef.current()` which stays updated on every render without changing the subscription’s dependency array.

lessons.title: React Server Components (RSC) & Boundaries
lessons.summary: React Server Components run solely on the server—accessing databases and heavy parsers with 0 KB shipped to the browser!

Interactive leaf components declare `"use client"`; Server Components can pass serializable props or rendered Server JSX as `children` into Client Components.
Push `"use client"` boundaries down to interactive leaves to keep browser bundles tiny.

interviewQA.question: Can a Client Component wrap a Server Component?

interviewQA.question: Primary performance benefit of RSC?
interviewQA.answer: Zero browser bundle cost for server-only logic and libraries (DB clients, markdown/syntax highlighters).

lessons.title: Accessibility Engineering & Live Regions
lessons.summary: Production React apps enforce semantic buttons/links, keyboard navigation, route focus/title updates, and permanently mounted `aria-live="polite"` toast regions.

interviewQA.question: Why avoid `<div onClick>`?

interviewQA.question: Why are `VITE_*` env vars unsafe for secret API keys?

lessons.title: React DevTools Profiler & Identifying Real Bottlenecks

commonMistakes.fix: Dev mode includes StrictMode double-renders; verify bottlenecks in production builds first.

explanation: A request waterfall happens when Parent fetches A, finishes, mounts Child, and ONLY THEN Child fetches B—doubling total wait time!
Eliminate waterfalls by fetching independent resources in parallel (`Promise.all([loadMeta(slug), loadLessons(slug), loadQuizzes(slug)])`) at the route boundary or preloading on hover/intent.
Show instant skeleton structure while parallel chunks resolve so perceived latency feels crisp.

Preload dynamic chunks on link hover/focus for near-instant transitions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fetching `meta`, awaiting, then fetching `lessons`, awaiting, then fetching `quizzes` sequentially
commonMistakes.fix: Start independent requests simultaneously with `Promise.all`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Blocking the entire course page on an optional PDF library import
commonMistakes.fix: Keep optional heavy modules lazy-loaded on click.

interviewQA.question: What is a React component request waterfall?
interviewQA.answer: When a parent fetches data before rendering a child that then initiates its own fetch, chaining network round trips sequentially instead of running them in parallel.

interviewQA.question: How do you eliminate waterfalls in a React SPA?
interviewQA.answer: Hoist parallel `Promise.all` fetches to the route/loader level and preload chunks on user intent.

lessons.title: Design-System Components, Variants & Focus Discipline
lessons.summary: Reusable UI primitives (`Button`, `Card`, `Badge`, `Modal`) separate semantic intent (`variant="primary" | "ghost"`) from one-off layout spacing, ensuring visual consistency across 15+ pages.
explanation: Reusable UI primitives (`Button`, `Card`, `Badge`, `Modal`) separate semantic intent (`variant="primary" | "ghost"`) from one-off layout spacing, ensuring visual consistency across 15+ pages.

Forward native HTML attributes (`ComponentPropsWithoutRef<"button">`), default `<button type="button">` so buttons inside forms never submit accidentally, and preserve crisp `:focus-visible` rings in both Light and Dark themes.
Never bake external margins (`mt-8`) into reusable primitives—let parent layouts control spacing with `gap`.

codeExample.title: Accessible Design-System Button Primitive

keyPoints: Default `type="button"` prevents accidental form submissions.
Parent grids/flexboxes own spacing (`gap`), not child margins.
Always pair light and dark tokens with WCAG AA contrast (>= 4.5:1).

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting `type="button"` on custom icon buttons inside `<form>`
commonMistakes.fix: HTML defaults `<button>` inside forms to `type="submit"`, triggering unexpected submits!

commonMistakes.mistake: Hardcoding `mb-6` inside a reusable `<Card>` component
commonMistakes.fix: Removes layout flexibility; let parent containers apply `gap-6` instead.

interviewQA.question: Why should reusable `<Button>` components default to `type="button"`?
interviewQA.answer: Because `<button>` inside a `<form>` defaults to `type="submit"`, so secondary buttons like "Cancel" or "Show Hint" will accidentally submit the form unless `type="button"` is set.

interviewQA.question: Why should reusable UI primitives avoid hardcoded outer margins?
interviewQA.answer: Margins leak layout assumptions; letting parent Flex/Grid containers manage spacing via `gap` keeps components portable anywhere.

lessons.title: Production Build Hygiene, Caching & State Persistence
lessons.summary: Production React SPAs rely on content-hashed Vite bundles, clean schema versioning for `localStorage`, and zero console/network errors.
explanation: Production React SPAs rely on content-hashed Vite bundles, clean schema versioning for `localStorage`, and zero console/network errors.
Version your client persistence key (`it_courses_state_v1`) and merge loaded JSON safely with defaults so adding a new feature field later never crashes returning learners!
Always verify rendered flows in a real browser across Desktop (1440px) and Mobile (390px) viewports in both Light and Dark themes.

codeExample.title: Forward-Compatible Versioned Storage Loader

keyPoints: Merge persisted JSON with default state to survive schema additions.
Content-hashed JS/CSS chunks enable immutable CDN caching.
Verify zero console errors, zero horizontal overflow, and full keyboard nav before shipping.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading `JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem(KEY)!)` with zero `try/catch` or default merge
commonMistakes.fix: Corrupted or older-schema storage crashes the app on boot; always merge safely with defaults.

commonMistakes.mistake: Never testing mobile 390px layouts or Dark mode contrast
commonMistakes.fix: Responsive overflows and dark-on-dark contrast bugs surface immediately in multi-viewport checks.

interviewQA.question: Why should client-side `localStorage` state be merged with default values on load?
interviewQA.answer: When a returning learner loads a newer app version that added new fields, merging `{ ...defaults, ...saved }` guarantees new properties are never `undefined`.

interviewQA.question: Why does Vite append content hashes like `index-9a8f2c.js` in `dist/`?
interviewQA.answer: So browsers and CDNs can cache assets aggressively forever while automatically fetching new hashes on every deploy.

sections.title: React Fiber Internals, Batching & Custom Renderers
sections.description: Understand Fiber trees, priority lanes, Suspense boundaries, and imperative interop.

lessons.title: Fiber Architecture & Double Buffering
lessons.summary: React Fiber models each component instance as a linked-list Fiber node (`child`, `sibling`, `return`) so React can pause, prioritize, and resume render work across frames.
explanation: React Fiber models each component instance as a linked-list Fiber node (`child`, `sibling`, `return`) so React can pause, prioritize, and resume render work across frames.
React keeps two Fiber trees (`current` on screen and `workInProgress` being built) and swaps a single pointer atomically during Commit—known as double buffering.
Understanding Fiber explains why render must stay pure (work-in-progress trees can be discarded and restarted on higher-priority clicks).

codeExample.title: Interruptible Pure Render Contract

keyPoints: Fiber replaces React’s old recursive call stack with interruptible linked-list units of work.
Double buffering swaps `workInProgress` into `current` atomically at Commit.
Priority lanes let urgent clicks preempt low-priority transitions.

commonMistakes.mistake: Incrementing a module-level counter during render
commonMistakes.fix: Interrupted renders and StrictMode run render multiple times, producing bogus counts.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming `setState` always runs synchronously before the next line
commonMistakes.fix: Updates schedule into priority lanes and commit asynchronously in batches.

interviewQA.question: What problem did React Fiber solve compared to React 15’s Stack Reconciler?
interviewQA.answer: Stack reconciliation was synchronous and uninterruptible, freezing the main thread on large updates; Fiber splits work into interruptible units with priority lanes.

interviewQA.question: What is Fiber double buffering?
interviewQA.answer: Building the next tree off-screen in `workInProgress` and flipping one root pointer on commit so the DOM never shows half-rendered states.

lessons.title: flushSync, Automatic Batching & Third-Party Imperative Widgets
lessons.summary: React 18/19 automatically batches multiple `setState` calls inside events, Promises, and timers into ONE render pass.
explanation: React 18/19 automatically batches multiple `setState` calls inside events, Promises, and timers into ONE render pass.
In rare cases where you need DOM updates committed synchronously before reading scrollHeight or calling `window.print()`, `flushSync(() => setState(...))` forces an immediate commit.
For imperative libraries like CodeMirror, Leaflet, or D3, mount the instance inside `useEffect` on a `ref` container and destroy it cleanly in the cleanup callback.

codeExample.title: Mounting an Imperative Library Safely in React

keyPoints: Automatic batching reduces unnecessary renders across async boundaries.
Use `flushSync` sparingly—it opts out of batching and concurrent optimizations.
Always destroy imperative third-party widget instances in effect cleanup.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling `flushSync` inside a render function or `useEffect`
commonMistakes.fix: Throws a React warning/error; only call `flushSync` inside event handlers when strictly required.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mounting CodeMirror or Chart.js without calling `.destroy()` in cleanup
commonMistakes.fix: StrictMode double-mount immediately creates TWO stacked editors in the same div!

interviewQA.question: What happens when integrating a third-party imperative library without cleanup under StrictMode?
interviewQA.answer: StrictMode mounts twice in dev, producing duplicated DOM widgets unless cleanup destroys the previous instance.

interviewQA.question: When is `flushSync` justified?
interviewQA.answer: Rare DOM-sync cases like scrolling immediately to a newly appended chat message or triggering `window.print()` right after revealing print content.

lessons.title: useImperativeHandle & Controlled Component APIs
lessons.summary: When a parent genuinely needs to invoke an imperative method on a child (like `playerRef.current.pause()` or `editorRef.current.reset()`), expose a narrow curated handle via `useImperativeHandle` rather than leaking the raw DOM node.
explanation: When a parent genuinely needs to invoke an imperative method on a child (like `playerRef.current.pause()` or `editorRef.current.reset()`), expose a narrow curated handle via `useImperativeHandle` rather than leaking the raw DOM node.
Keep declarative props as the primary API (95% of cases) and reserve imperative handles for media playback, focus, scroll-to-row, or form reset.
Always pass the dependency array to `useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ ... }), [deps])`.

codeExample.title: Exposing a Narrow Imperative Handle

keyPoints: `useImperativeHandle` restricts what parents can invoke on a child ref.
Prevents tight coupling to internal DOM structure.
In React 19, `ref` is received directly as a normal prop.

commonMistakes.mistake: Exposing imperative `.setValue()` methods for data that should simply be controlled via props
commonMistakes.fix: Prefer declarative `value` + `onChange` props; use imperative handles only for actions like `.focus()` or `.scrollIntoView()`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaking raw internal DOM nodes from complex design-system components
commonMistakes.fix: Expose a small typed handle interface instead.

interviewQA.question: When is `useImperativeHandle` preferred over declarative props?
interviewQA.answer: For non-declarative browser actions like `.focus()`, `.play()`, `.scrollToIndex()`, or `.selectText()`.

interviewQA.question: What does `useImperativeHandle` protect against?
interviewQA.answer: Parents mutating internal DOM styles or attributes directly in ways that break component invariants.

lessons.title: React 19 `use()` API & Reading Promises/Context Conditionally
lessons.summary: React 19’s `use(resource)` hook reads the resolved value of a Promise (suspending via nearest `<Suspense>`) or reads a Context—and UNLIKE every other hook, `use()` CAN be called inside `if` statements and loops!
explanation: React 19’s `use(resource)` hook reads the resolved value of a Promise (suspending via nearest `<Suspense>`) or reads a Context—and UNLIKE every other hook, `use()` CAN be called inside `if` statements and loops!
Create/cache the Promise outside render (in a loader, cache, or Server Component) rather than calling `fetch()` fresh inside render, or every re-render suspends endlessly.
Combine `<ErrorBoundary>` + `<Suspense>` + `use(promise)` for crisp declarative async trees.

codeExample.title: Conditional Context Read with React 19 `use()`

keyPoints: `use(promise)` integrates with `<Suspense>` and `<ErrorBoundary>` seamlessly.
`use()` is the ONLY React API allowed inside `if` blocks and loops.
Never create an uncached Promise directly inside render passed to `use()`.

commonMistakes.mistake: Writing `const data = use(fetch("/api/x"))` directly inside a component body
commonMistakes.fix: Every render creates a brand-new pending Promise, causing an infinite Suspense loop; hoist or cache the Promise!

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting an Error Boundary around `use(promise)`
commonMistakes.fix: Rejected Promises bubble to the nearest Error Boundary cleanly.

interviewQA.question: How does React 19’s `use(Context)` differ from `useContext(Context)`?
interviewQA.answer: `use()` can be called conditionally inside `if` branches or loops after early returns, whereas `useContext()` must follow strict top-level hook ordering.

interviewQA.question: What happens when a Promise passed to `use(promise)` rejects?
interviewQA.answer: React catches the rejection and displays the fallback of the nearest parent Error Boundary.

sections.title: Production React Engineering: State Libraries, Animations & i18n
sections.description: Choose right-sized state tools, build accessible motion, handle internationalization, and ship zero-defect builds.

lessons.title: Choosing State Management: Context vs Zustand vs TanStack Query
lessons.summary: Not all state belongs in one tool: TanStack Query/SWR owns remote server cache (deduplication, retries, background refetch), URL searchParams own navigation filters, and Zustand or Context+useReducer own client UI state.
explanation: Not all state belongs in one tool: TanStack Query/SWR owns remote server cache (deduplication, retries, background refetch), URL searchParams own navigation filters, and Zustand or Context+useReducer own client UI state.
Selector-based stores (like Zustand `useStore(s => s.streak)`) let components subscribe to ONE atomic slice without re-rendering when unrelated store keys change.
Start simple with local state + Context + adapter services; reach for external stores only when Context fan-out or server-cache complexity genuinely warrants them.

codeExample.title: Atomic Selector Pattern Concept

keyPoints: Separate server cache state from local/global UI state.
Selector subscriptions re-render ONLY when the selected slice changes.
Avoid reaching for heavy global stores before measuring real need.

commonMistakes.mistake: Copying REST API responses manually into Redux/Context with hand-rolled loading flags everywhere
commonMistakes.fix: Server-cache libraries handle caching, deduplication, and background refresh automatically.

commonMistakes.mistake: Storing transient form input keystrokes in a global store
commonMistakes.fix: Keep form drafts local to the form component.

interviewQA.question: Why is Server Cache state fundamentally different from Client UI state?
interviewQA.answer: Server data is asynchronous, shared, potentially stale, and owned remotely—needing caching, deduplication, and revalidation rather than plain local setters.

interviewQA.question: How do selector-based stores prevent unnecessary re-renders compared to plain Context?
interviewQA.answer: Each subscriber compares only its selected slice (`s => s.count`) with `Object.is`, skipping renders when other store properties update.

lessons.title: Smooth, Accessible Micro-Interactions & Motion
lessons.summary: Purposeful motion clarifies state transitions (drawer slide, quiz progress bar fill, card elevation) using compositor-only properties (`transform`, `opacity`) while respecting `prefers-reduced-motion`.
explanation: Purposeful motion clarifies state transitions (drawer slide, quiz progress bar fill, card elevation) using compositor-only properties (`transform`, `opacity`) while respecting `prefers-reduced-motion`.
Never animate layout-triggering properties like `width`, `height`, or `top` on hot 60fps loops—animate `transform: scaleX()` or `translateY()` instead, and keep UI transitions brisk (150ms–250ms).
Provide reduced-motion alternatives so vestibular-sensitive learners experience crisp instant transitions with zero dizziness.

codeExample.title: GPU-Composited Progress Bar & Reduced-Motion Respect

keyPoints: Animate `transform` and `opacity` for 60fps GPU-composited motion.
Use Tailwind `motion-reduce:transition-none` to respect OS reduced-motion preferences.
Keep UI micro-interactions crisp (150–250ms), never sluggish or distracting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Animating `width: 0% -> 100%` continuously on 23 cards at once
commonMistakes.fix: Triggers layout recalculation every frame; animate `transform: scaleX()` instead.

commonMistakes.mistake: Adding infinite pulsing/bouncing animations on static buttons or status dots
commonMistakes.fix: Distracts readers and violates accessibility comfort; reserve motion for meaningful state changes.

interviewQA.question: Why is animating `transform: scaleX()` faster than animating `width`?
interviewQA.answer: `transform` runs purely on the GPU compositor thread without triggering browser Layout or Paint passes.

interviewQA.question: How does Tailwind CSS support `prefers-reduced-motion`?
interviewQA.answer: With the `motion-reduce:` and `motion-safe:` variants (e.g., `motion-reduce:transition-none`).

lessons.title: Internationalization (i18n), Formatting & RTL Readiness
lessons.summary: Build React apps ready for global learners by formatting dates/numbers with native `Intl`, isolating copy cleanly, and using Tailwind logical utilities (`ms-`, `me-`, `ps-`, `pe-`, `text-start`) so RTL locales mirror seamlessly.
explanation: Build React apps ready for global learners by formatting dates/numbers with native `Intl`, isolating copy cleanly, and using Tailwind logical utilities (`ms-`, `me-`, `ps-`, `pe-`, `text-start`) so RTL locales mirror seamlessly.

Never concatenate translated fragments (`t("completed") + " " + n + " " + t("lessons")`) because word order and pluralization differ wildly across languages—use parameterized message templates (`"{count} lessons completed"`).
Keep numbers aligned vertically in dashboards using `tabular-nums` (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`).

codeExample.title: Locale-Safe Formatting with Native Intl

keyPoints: Use `Intl.DateTimeFormat` and `Intl.NumberFormat` instead of hardcoded US date strings.
Use Tailwind logical spacing (`ps-4`, `text-start`) for automatic RTL readiness.
Apply `tabular-nums` on timers, quiz counters, and dashboard stats so digits never jitter.

commonMistakes.mistake: Hardcoding `"MM/DD/YYYY"` with `getMonth() + 1` everywhere
commonMistakes.fix: Use `Intl.DateTimeFormat(undefined, { dateStyle: "medium" })` for clean locale-aware dates.

commonMistakes.mistake: Omitting `tabular-nums` on countdown exam timers
commonMistakes.fix: Proportional fonts jump horizontally every second (`1` vs `8`); `tabular-nums` locks digit widths.

interviewQA.question: Why is `tabular-nums` essential on countdown timers and dashboard metrics?
interviewQA.answer: Proportional digits vary in width so ticking timers jitter left and right; `tabular-nums` gives every digit identical monospace width cleanly inside a sans-serif font.

interviewQA.question: Why should i18n strings use full parameterized templates instead of string concatenation?
interviewQA.answer: Different languages place subjects, counts, and verbs in different orders and have complex plural forms.

lessons.title: End-to-End Verification & Real-Browser Quality Gates
lessons.summary: Before shipping any React application, verify it end-to-end in a real headless browser across Desktop and Mobile viewports, Light and Dark modes, checking zero console/network errors and full interactive flows.
explanation: Before shipping any React application, verify it end-to-end in a real headless browser across Desktop and Mobile viewports, Light and Dark modes, checking zero console/network errors and full interactive flows.
Combine static checks (`tsc --noEmit` + `eslint`), unit tests (`node:test`), production build (`vite build`), and real-browser Playwright checks so regressions never reach learners.
Inspect real rendered screenshots visually—layout overlaps, clipped text, broken dark-mode contrast, and dead buttons stand out immediately in screenshots.

codeExample.title: Complete Production Quality Gate Checklist

keyPoints: Zero TypeScript errors does NOT guarantee zero runtime/layout bugs—always test in a real browser.
Verify both Light and Dark modes plus narrow 390px mobile screens for horizontal overflow.
Check console errors, failed image/asset requests, and interactive forms end-to-end.

commonMistakes.mistake: Shipping after `npm run build` without opening the running app in a browser
commonMistakes.fix: Runtime errors, missing assets, broken z-index overlaps, and dark-mode contrast issues only show up at runtime.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only checking the landing page and skipping inner routes like quizzes, exams, and PDF exports
commonMistakes.fix: Walk every critical learner journey end-to-end before release.

interviewQA.question: Why is `npm run build` alone insufficient to guarantee a working React release?
interviewQA.answer: Builds verify syntax and bundling, not runtime data loading, CSS layout overflow, dark-mode contrast, or broken event handlers.

interviewQA.question: What should an automated browser smoke test assert on every route?
interviewQA.answer: Zero `console.error` / `pageerror`, HTTP 200 on assets, `scrollWidth <= innerWidth` (no horizontal overflow), and working primary interactive actions.
